author: SAT - International
title: New Crime Survey Reveals Widespread Under-Reporting and 'Trust Deficit' in South Africa
text:
A sobering new Victims of Crime Survey has exposed a significant gap between official police statistics and the lived experiences of South Africans, pointing to a deep “trust deficit” in the country’s criminal justice system and a complex web of reasons why crimes go unreported.
The survey, released by Statistics South Africa, is designed to capture the “dark figure of crime”—offenses that are never reported to authorities. While official police data showed a slight decrease in housebreaking incidents year-on-year, the survey suggests the true scale of crime and its impact is far greater.
In an interview, Dr. Mpho Matlala, a senior lecturer in Police Practice at the University of South Africa (UNISA), cautioned that the minor decreases are “insignificant” to victims. “A person’s home is supposed to be a sanctuary… even if we decrease those crimes to 0.1%, it is 0.1% too many,” Dr. Matlala stated.
The core issue, according to Dr. Matlala, is a pervasive under-reporting of crimes, driven primarily by a lack of public confidence in the police, prosecutions, and courts. However, he elaborated that the reasons extend beyond a simple trust deficit.
“For example, in sexual offenses, some people will be dissuaded by family members not to report,” he explained. Other factors include protecting marriages, financial dependency on the perpetrator, and deep-seated cultural, religious, and social stigmas that lead to feelings of shame and a fear of judgment.
The discussion turned to national leadership, with the interviewer questioning whether the current government has the will to address rampant crime, citing recent political turmoil and suspensions within the Department of Justice.
Dr. Matlala agreed that a leadership problem exists, but pinpointed a more systemic failure: a flawed, non-empirical approach to policing strategy. He revealed that crucial reports like the Victims of Crime Survey are largely ignored by police leadership when crafting crime-fighting plans.
“The approach is flawed because it’s non-empirical. It is not scientific,” Dr. Matlala said. “Statistics are there… but in terms of formulating targeted strategies that are informed by empirical evidence such as this report, that is where we are lacking.”
He attributed this failure to a critical skills gap within the top echelons of police management, suggesting that many senior officials lack the advanced analytical training required to interpret complex data and synthesize it into effective action.
“The criteria is such that you probably will get generals with national diplomas… to be able to interpret a report such as this one, you probably will need to have a master’s or a doctoral degree,” he argued. He concluded that South African policing has failed to modernize and remains stuck in the past, unable to meet the needs of a democratic state.
The survey paints a picture of a nation not only grappling with crime itself, but also with a profound crisis of confidence in the very institutions meant to ensure its safety.
